prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how different kinds of DNA damage trigger repair pathways and cell-cycle checkpoints across G1, S, G2, and M phases. Along the top, various stresses and treatments—such as ROS, irradiation, TMZ, cisplatin, TOP inhibitors, UV, and replication stress—are shown producing lesions including single-strand breaks, DNA base damage, DNA double-strand breaks, interstrand crosslinks, and stalled replication forks.

These lesions feed into a network of repair mechanisms, including BER, NER, homologous recombination, non-homologous end joining, alternative NHEJ, translesion synthesis, and Fanconi anemia-related repair. Central signaling kinases ATM and ATR connect damage sensing to downstream checkpoint control, with CHK2, CHK1, p53, WEE1, and related regulators slowing CDK activity to enforce G1 or S/G2/M arrest.

A major theme is the repeated placement of PRMT5 and several other proteins in pink near many branches of the network, suggesting they modulate multiple repair and checkpoint responses. Proteins like RAD51, WRN, DNA-PK, Pol θ, FANCD2, and PARP also appear at specific repair nodes. On the right, unresolved damage is linked to cytosolic double-stranded DNA, micronuclei, and activation of cGAS–STING interferon signaling, connecting defective repair to immune responses.
